Southern American English encompasses the accents and dialects of the American South, ranging from conservative plantation-influenced speech to modern urban Southern. Marked by distinctive prosody with melodic speech patterns, vowel shifts like the Southern Shift, and grammatical features including double modals, it carries strong regional identity and cultural associations.

The most notable phonological feature is the Southern Shift, a systematic fronting of back vowels and backing of front vowels. This makes "fleece" sound more like "flice" and "face" toward "fice." Monophthongization of i and oi sounds occurs, so "time" becomes "tahm" and "oil" sounds like "ahl."

Another feature is intrusive r insertion, adding an r sound between vowels in words like "idea," pronounced "idear." Southern English uses "y'all," from "you all," as a plural second-person pronoun, and "ain't" as a general negative, shared with AAVE.

Double modals are constructions like "might could" or "might would" that are ungrammatical in standard English but characteristic of Southern speech. Rhoticity, the pronunciation of r, varies regionally. Traditional coastal Southern may be non-rhotic, while inland Southern is typically rhotic.

Southern American English diverges systematically from General American, the prestige American standard. It shares historical roots in the South and some phonological patterns with AAVE, though with distinct grammatical features. Appalachian English, a regional variant within broader Southern speech, preserves additional archaic features.
